questions.q: What does the `with sharing` Apex keyword actually enforce?
options: The running user's record-sharing rules (OWD, role hierarchy, sharing rules) inside that class's queries and DML
Field-level security for every field on the object
API rate limits for the running user
Password complexity rules for the running user
questions.explain: `with sharing` enforces record-level sharing rules -- which records the running user can see -- inside that class's logic. It does not, by itself, enforce object or field-level permissions, which is a separate check.

questions.q: By default, does Apex automatically enforce object and field-level security (CRUD/FLS) for the running user?
options: Yes, Apex always enforces CRUD/FLS automatically regardless of any keyword used
No -- Apex runs in system context by default, so a query or DML statement can succeed even if the running user's profile lacks access to the object or field, unless CRUD/FLS is enforced explicitly
Only `without sharing` classes skip CRUD/FLS enforcement; `with sharing` classes enforce it automatically
CRUD/FLS enforcement was removed from the Apex language entirely
questions.explain: Sharing and CRUD/FLS are separate checks. Apex runs in system context by default, so CRUD/FLS has to be enforced deliberately -- via WITH USER_MODE, AccessLevel.USER_MODE, WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED, explicit isAccessible()/isCreateable() checks, or Security.stripInaccessible().

questions.q: What makes the `inherited sharing` keyword useful for a reusable utility class, per this lesson?
options: It permanently disables sharing enforcement for any class that uses it
It automatically rewrites any SOQL injection vulnerabilities in the class
It gives the class a safe with-sharing default when it's the actual entry point into Apex, while still running without sharing if explicitly called from an already-without-sharing context
It is identical in every respect to declaring `without sharing`
questions.explain: `inherited sharing` runs as with sharing at entry points (e.g., an @AuraEnabled method called from a Lightning Web Component), but defers to without sharing only when called from a context that was already without sharing -- a safer default for code that might get reused in contexts the original author never anticipated.

questions.q: What is SOQL injection, and what is the standard fix for it?
options: A governor limit violation caused by too many SOQL queries in one transaction; fixed by bulkifying the code
An error caused by querying a field that doesn't exist on an object
A deprecated Apex feature that no longer poses any risk
Building a SOQL query by concatenating unescaped, untrusted user input, which lets an attacker alter the query's behavior; fixed by using bind variables instead of string concatenation
questions.explain: SOQL injection is the same category of risk as classic SQL injection -- concatenating untrusted input into a query string lets an attacker change what the query does. Bind variables (:variableName) are the standard fix, with String.escapeSingleQuotes() as a fallback when dynamic SOQL can't be avoided.

questions.q: In the Lab scenario, a `without sharing` class written for a legitimate nightly batch job gets reused 18 months later by a new Lightning Web Component feature. What authorization gap does this reuse create?
options: The support agent's UI feature now bypasses record-sharing rules it was never meant to bypass, because it's calling code that ignores sharing entirely regardless of who invokes it
No gap is created -- `without sharing` behavior only ever applies to batch jobs, never to UI-triggered calls
The reuse automatically triggers a SOQL injection vulnerability
The reuse causes the batch job to stop working entirely
questions.explain: Because `without sharing` ignores sharing rules for whoever calls the class, reusing that code from a new, UI-triggered feature silently gives the calling feature the same unrestricted record access the batch job needed -- an authorization gap nobody designed for, and exactly the kind of risk `inherited sharing` is meant to prevent.
